items.abstract: <jats:p>The proliferation of 5G and Internet of Things (IoT) edge networks has exponentially increased the attack surface for covert exfiltration channels, with DNS tunneling remaining one of the most insidious due to its ability to bypass traditional firewall inspection. Existing detection mechanisms, predominantly rule-based or reliant on shallow machine learning, struggle to generalize against zero-day tunneling variants that exploit the high-throughput, low-latency characteristics of 5G and the resource-constrained heterogeneity of IoT devices. This research introduces a novel hybrid deep learning framework that synergizes Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Transformer architectures to detect novel DNS tunneling signatures in real-time at the network edge. The proposed model leverages GNNs to model the structural and temporal dependencies of DNS query-response interactions across distributed edge nodes, capturing relational patterns and anomalous propagation behaviors that are invisible to per-flow analyzers. Concurrently, a multi-head Transformer encoder is employed to process the sequential payload embeddings and query-name character distributions, enabling the capture of long-range semantic anomalies and obfuscation strategies characteristic of advanced tunneling tools. By fusing the relational reasoning of GNNs with the sequential context awareness of Transformers, our approach achieves a dual-faceted representation of both network topology dynamics and per-query syntactic deviations. Preliminary evaluations on a custom 5G-IoT edge testbed, incorporating both known and evolving zero-day tunneling payloads, demonstrate a significant improvement in detection accuracy and a marked reduction in false positive rates compared to isolated models. This framework not only addresses the limitations of signature-based systems but also provides an adaptive, explainable mechanism for securing next-generation edge infrastructures against sophisticated data exfiltration attacks.</jats:p>
title: Using Hybrid Neural Networks (Graph Neural Networks + Transformers) to Detect Novel DNS Tunneling Signatures in 5G and IoT Edge Networks

items.abstract: <jats:p>Recent research on graph neural networks (GNNs) has explored mechanisms for capturing local uncertainty and exploiting graph hierarchies to mitigate data sparsity and leverage structural properties. However, the synergistic integration of these two approaches remains underexplored. This work introduces a novel architecture, the Hierarchy- and Uncertainty-aware Graph Neural Networks (HUGNN), which unifies multi-scale representation learning, principled uncertainty estimation, and self-supervised embedding diversity within a single end-to-end framework. Specifically, HU-GNN adaptively forms node clusters and estimates uncertainty at multiple structural scales from individual nodes to higher levels. These uncertainty estimates guide a robust message-passing mechanism and attentionweighting, effectively mitigating noise and adversarial perturbations while preserving predictive accuracy on semi-supervised classification tasks. We provide key theoretical contributions, including a probabilistic formulation, rigorous uncertaintycalibration guarantees, and formal robustness bounds. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art robustness and interpretability.</jats:p>
title: Hierarchical and Uncertainty-Aware Graph Neural Networks for Heterophily and Robustness

items.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are increasingly used to model protein–protein interaction networks in cancer biology but are commonly deployed using central ized, cloud-based GPU infrastructure. This study examines the computational feasibility and numerical stability of executing GNN training and inference on decentralized, GPU-accelerated edge computing platforms. Using a protein protein interaction network comprising 1,603 genes and transcriptomic data from TCGA breast and lung cancer cohorts, we evaluate convergence behavior, mem ory constraints, and inference latency on a Jetson-class Single Board Computer. To avoid conflating hardware validation with biological performance, experiments are explicitly separated into (i) synthetic graph signal stress tests for systems level evaluation and (ii) biologically unmodified TCGA benchmarks for baseline predictive assessment. Results demonstrate stable convergence, tightly bounded inference latency (˜15 ms), and baseline predictive performance consistent with prior network-based oncology studies. These findings indicate that edge-based platforms can support graph neural network execution for molecular network analysis without reliance on centralized computing infrastructure.
title: Edge-Based Execution of Graph Neural Networks for Protein Interaction Network Analysis in Clinical Oncology
